title: Honor Killing, FGM, and Culture vs. Religion
summary: A direct, unambiguous look at two practices sometimes associated with Islam in Western media — what Islamic scripture and mainstream scholarship actually say about them, and where they really come from.

body.text: Honor killing and female genital mutilation (FGM) are both real, documented practices in some communities that include Muslims, and both are sometimes described in Western media as "Islamic practices." This lesson addresses both directly and specifically, rather than vaguely — because a vague answer here tends to sound evasive, and this deserves a clear one.
Honor killing: not an Islamic teaching

There is no basis in the Quran or authentic hadith for killing a family member over perceived "dishonour" — none of the primary sources sanction it, and it directly contradicts the general Islamic prohibition on murder covered in the lesson on violence, as well as the strict legal process Islamic law requires before any punishment can be carried out for any offence (a legitimate court, evidence, due process — never private, extrajudicial killing by a family member). Mainstream Islamic scholars and institutions worldwide, including in countries where honor killings occur, condemn the practice explicitly and describe it as a pre-Islamic tribal custom that persists in some regions, cutting across religious lines — it also occurs among non-Muslim communities in the same regions, which is itself evidence the practice is cultural and regional rather than religious in origin.

body.translation: Whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely.

body.text: FGM: also not an Islamic teaching

Female genital mutilation is not mentioned in the Quran at all, and is not practised by the majority of the world's Muslims — it's concentrated in specific regions (parts of Africa particularly) and is practised there by Muslims, Christians, and followers of traditional religions alike, which again points to a regional cultural origin predating Islam rather than a religious one. Major Islamic institutions, including Al-Azhar University (one of the most authoritative centres of Sunni scholarship) and numerous national fatwa councils, have explicitly condemned the practice and issued rulings against it, citing its serious, well-documented physical and psychological harm.
Why "culture vs. religion" isn't a dodge here

It can sound like a convenient excuse to say "that's culture, not religion" — so it's worth being specific about why that distinction holds up here rather than just asserting it: both practices predate Islam in the regions where they occur, both occur among non-Muslims in those same regions, both lack any basis in the Quran or authentic hadith, and both are explicitly condemned by mainstream Islamic religious authorities, not just quietly ignored. That combination is what makes this a genuine culture/religion distinction, not a rhetorical shortcut.

It's possible, and more honest, to hold both of these at the same time: these practices are real, harmful, and occur in some Muslim communities, and they are not Islamic teachings and are explicitly rejected by mainstream Islamic scholarship. Neither point cancels the other out.

body.question: What if someone says "but it happens in Muslim countries, so it must be Islamic"?
body.answer: A practice occurring in a Muslim-majority country doesn't make it Islamic, any more than a harmful practice occurring in a majority-Christian country makes it Christian — the relevant question is what the religion's actual texts and mainstream scholarship say, which in both these cases is a clear, documented rejection.

body.question: Where can someone learn more or find help if this is personally relevant to them or someone they know?
body.answer: This is a serious safeguarding matter, not just a talking point — if you or someone you know is at risk, contact local domestic violence, forced marriage, or FGM protection services in your country directly; in the UK, for example, the Forced Marriage Unit and NSPCC's FGM helpline are established resources. A knowledgeable, safeguarding-trained imam can also help, but professional support services should be the first point of contact for actual risk.
